Every Current Creates a Magnetic Field

Sections 28.2–28.4 answered: given \(\vec{B}\), what force does it exert? We now ask the complementary question: given a current, what \(\vec{B}\) does it create? The answer was established by Biot and Savart in 1820. The Biot-Savart Law gives the infinitesimal field at point P due to a current element \(I\,d\vec{\ell}\):

\[\boxed{d\vec{B} = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{I\,d\vec{\ell}\times\hat{r}}{r^2}}\]

where \(\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \text{T}\cdot\text{m/A}\) is the permeability of free space, \(d\vec{\ell}\) points along the current, \(\hat{r}\) points from element to field point, and \(r\) is the distance. Total field: \(\vec{B} = \int d\vec{B}\).

Structural Parallel — Biot-Savart and Coulomb

Property Coulomb’s Law (Ch 22) Biot-Savart Law (Ch 28)
Source Point charge \(dq\) Current element \(I\,d\vec{\ell}\)
Field \(d\vec{E} = k_e\,dq\,\hat{r}/r^2\) \(d\vec{B} = (\mu_0/4\pi)\,I\,d\vec{\ell}\times\hat{r}/r^2\)
Direction Along \(\hat{r}\) (radial) \(\perp\) to both \(d\vec{\ell}\) and \(\hat{r}\)
\(1/r^2\) dependence Yes Yes

The key difference: \(\vec{E}\) points radially outward; \(\vec{B}\) circulates around the wire. This is why magnetic field lines form loops rather than radiating outward.

Field of an Infinite Straight Wire

Integrating the Biot-Savart Law along an infinite wire (the same integration-along-a-line technique used for charged rods in Chapter 23):

\[\boxed{B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}}\]

The field circulates around the wire in closed circles, with direction given by the right-hand rule: thumb along current, fingers curl in the direction of \(\vec{B}\).

The \(1/r\) dependence — not \(1/r^2\) — matches the electric field of an infinite line charge (\(E = \lambda/2\pi\varepsilon_0 r\) from Ch 23). The slower falloff reflects the 1D source geometry: every point along the infinite wire contributes.

Field on the Axis of a Circular Loop

For a loop of radius \(R\) carrying current \(I\), the on-axis field at distance \(x\) from center:

\[\boxed{B = \frac{\mu_0 I R^2}{2(R^2 + x^2)^{3/2}}}\]

Figure 28.6: Magnetic field of a circular current loop. Left: On-axis field. Right: Field lines — every line is a closed curve.

Limiting cases: At the center (\(x = 0\)): \(B = \mu_0 I/(2R)\) — the maximum on-axis value. Far from the loop (\(x \gg R\)): \(B \approx \mu_0 IR^2/(2x^3) \propto 1/x^3\) — the dipole falloff, the same \(1/r^3\) dependence we found for the electric field far from an electric dipole in Chapter 22. The current loop IS a magnetic dipole.

Example: Fields from a Coil and a Wire

(A) A 50-turn coil (\(R = 0.10\ \text{m}\), \(I = 2.0\ \text{A}\)). At center: \(B = N\mu_0 I/(2R) = (50)(4\pi\times10^{-7})(2.0)/(0.20) = \boxed{0.63\ \text{mT}}\) — about 12× Earth’s field. A modest coil already dominates the local magnetic environment.

(B) A long wire (\(I = 5.0\ \text{A}\)) at \(r = 0.10\ \text{m}\): \(B = \mu_0 I/(2\pi r) = \boxed{10\ \mu\text{T}}\) — comparable to Earth’s field. At \(r = 0.050\ \text{m}\), \(B = 20\ \mu\text{T}\). The \(1/r\) dependence is linear, not quadratic.
